title: Are HR generalists exempt from overtime: classification analysis for Mac users
metaTitle: Are HR generalists exempt? A guide to FLSA classification for HR
description: Are HR generalists exempt from FLSA overtime rules? Learn how to perform accurate classification analysis, mitigate legal risks, and manage documentation on your Mac.
intro: HR generalists often ask if they are exempt from overtime rules under the Fair Labor Standards Act. The answer depends entirely on your specific job duties and salary, not just your title or degree. You must satisfy both the salary basis test and the specific duties test for your role.
tldr: Classification depends on duties, not just job titles.
The employer carries the burden of proof for all exemptions.
Misclassification can lead to back wages and double damages.
Regular audits and documentation are your best defense.
State laws often impose stricter rules than federal standards.

blocks.text: Why FLSA classification analysis is a constant challenge

The FLSA landscape is complex because it relies on outdated regulatory frameworks. You cannot simply label a role as exempt. You must analyze the actual day to day work performed by the employee. Many HR generalists struggle because they assume a college degree or a professional title qualifies a role for exemption. This is a common mistake. The law focuses on whether the employee performs exempt duties like executive, administrative, or professional tasks as their primary function.

Regulatory agencies do not care about your internal job descriptions if they do not match reality. If you are performing mostly clerical or manual work, you are likely non-exempt. This creates a significant administrative burden. You must conduct interviews with managers and employees to understand the real work. You then compare those findings against the specific tests provided by the Department of Labor. This takes hours of time for every single position in your organization.

The financial risks of getting this wrong are severe. If you misclassify an employee, you owe them back wages for all unpaid overtime. The government can look back two years for standard errors. If they find your violation was willful, they can look back three years. You will often face liquidated damages. These essentially double the amount you owe to the employee. This can quickly turn a small error into a company threatening financial liability.
How to perform an FLSA audit on your Mac

You need a consistent process to protect your company. Start by creating a spreadsheet in Excel to track your findings. List every role and the date of its last classification review. Use a standard template to document the rationale for each decision. This audit trail is your primary defense if an investigator comes calling. You should review these classifications at least once a year or whenever a role changes significantly.

items: Create a master list of all current job descriptions in Word.
Review each role against the DOL duties test criteria.
Document the specific tasks that justify an exempt status.
Verify the salary level against current federal and state thresholds.
Store all final classification reports in a secure, searchable folder.

blocks.text: Always check your state labor laws. States like California and New York have higher salary thresholds and more restrictive duties tests than federal law. Federal compliance does not guarantee state compliance.
blocks.title: State law caveat

blocks.text: Several web based tools can help you manage this analysis. Tools like Exemptly or the Clockspot FLSA analyzer provide guided questionnaires. They help you walk through the federal criteria systematically. If you work at a larger company, tools like the ERI Occupational Assessor allow you to compare your roles against thousands of benchmarks. These tools do not replace legal advice, but they provide a structured way to handle the volume of work.

faq.question: Can I just copy a job description from another company?
faq.answer: No. You must classify based on the actual duties performed in your specific organization. Copying a description that does not reflect reality is a common cause of misclassification.

faq.question: What if the employee wants to be exempt?
faq.answer: Exemption status is not a choice. You cannot waive FLSA rights by agreement. Even if an employee prefers to be exempt, you must classify them correctly based on the law.

faq.question: How often should I review classifications?
faq.answer: Perform a review at least annually. You should also conduct a review whenever a role changes, a manager changes, or when federal or state salary thresholds increase.

costs.title: Administrative time
costs.text: Manual audits require hours of interviewing and documentation per role.

causes.title: Outdated regulations
causes.text: Modern roles do not always fit neatly into the administrative or executive buckets.

causes.title: Title bias
causes.text: Assuming that a specific job title or degree automatically confers exempt status.

causes.title: Lack of documentation
causes.text: Failing to maintain a clear record of why a role was classified a certain way.

fixes.title: Standardized audit process
fixes.text: Use a consistent checklist for every role to ensure nothing is missed.

fixes.title: Manager training
fixes.text: Educate hiring managers on FLSA basics before they set job expectations.

fixes.title: Audit trail creation
fixes.text: Document the specific duties that justify each classification decision in writing.
